title: How Long Is the Coast of Britain? Statistical Self-Similarity and Fractional Dimension
summary: In a 1967 Science paper, Benoit Mandelbrot argued that the lengths of coastlines are typically undefinable because such curves are statistically self-similar, and that their complication is measured by a fractional exponent D, reading Lewis Fry Richardson's measurements as giving D = 1.25 for the west coast of Great Britain.
body: Benoit Mandelbrot's paper, published in Science on 5 May 1967 (vol. 156, pp. 636-638), states that geographical curves are so involved in their detail that their lengths are "often infinite or more accurately, undefinable". It calls curves whose portions are, in a statistical sense, reduced-scale images of the whole statistically self-similar, and characterizes them by a similarity exponent D with many properties of a dimension, though a fractional one exceeding the value 1 of ordinary curves. Re-examining empirical observations from Richardson 1961, Mandelbrot interprets the data as implying that the dimension of the west coast of Great Britain is D = 1.25.
